faqs.q: What should I include on a general contractor estimate?
faqs.a: At minimum: your business name and license number, the client and job-site address, dated line items for materials, subcontractors, labor, permits, equipment and cleanup, a valid-until date, deposit terms and exclusions. Most states require a contractor license number on client-facing documents.

faqs.q: Is this template free to use?
faqs.a: Yes. All three formats (PDF, Word, Excel) are free to download with no email required.

faqs.q: Does the Excel version calculate the deposit and balance automatically?
faqs.a: Yes. Enter your quantity and rate per line, and the subtotal, 25% deposit and balance due update automatically.

faqs.q: Is this a contractor estimate form or a full estimate template?
faqs.a: It is both. This contractor estimate form works as a quick one-page estimate or a detailed multi-line template - it includes fields for labor, materials, permits, and subcontractor costs. Download as PDF for a printable form, or Excel for auto-calculating totals. No email required.

faqs.q: Is this legal or tax advice?
faqs.a: No. Templates are for informational purposes only. Requirements vary by state — verify with your contractor board and a CPA or attorney before use.

deepDive.heading: General contractor estimates: cost-plus vs fixed price, allowances and retainage
deepDive.sub: A GC estimate is a contract framework as much as a price. These are the mechanisms — allowances, schedule of values, retainage, change orders — that decide whether the job is profitable.

blocks.h3: Cost-plus or fixed price — the choice changes everything downstream
paras: A fixed-price estimate transfers risk to the contractor: if framing lumber rises or the crew takes longer, the GC absorbs it. A cost-plus estimate passes those through with a markup — typically 10 to 20 percent on materials and labour, sometimes a flat fee instead. Customers prefer fixed price; contractors prefer cost-plus on renovation where concealed conditions are likely.

The hybrid most renovations actually use is fixed price with allowances and a defined change-order process. That gives the customer a number they can finance, while keeping the unknowns adjustable rather than absorbed.
list: Fixed price: risk on the contractor, allowances and change orders define the edges
Cost-plus: open-book costs plus a stated markup or fee
Not-to-exceed: cost-plus with a ceiling the customer can rely on
Markup stated per category (materials, labour, subcontractors)

blocks.h3: Allowances are where estimates go wrong in both directions
paras: Allowances cover selections not yet made: tile, fixtures, lighting, appliances, cabinetry. Set them too low and the customer faces a large upcharge at selection time, which feels like a bait-and-switch even when it is documented. Set them too high and the estimate looks uncompetitive against a rival who assumed cheap finishes.

Price allowances at realistic mid-market numbers for the neighbourhood, list each one separately with its scope, and state the credit-or-charge rule. A GC who says "tile allowance $12/sq ft, plus installation" gives the customer a number they can shop against; one who says "tile included" is heading for a change-order fight.
list: Each allowance itemized with a dollar amount and unit basis
Credit if the customer selects below the allowance
Charge as a change order if above
Selection deadline tied to the schedule

blocks.h3: Schedule of values and progress billing
paras: On anything larger than a small remodel, billing is by schedule of values: the contract sum split into line items by phase (demo, foundation, framing, mechanical, finishes), each billed as it is completed. This is the mechanism that lets a GC carry material costs without financing the whole job.

Lenders and homeowners both expect it, and it makes the retainage conversation natural. Progress billing also forces discipline about what "complete" means for each phase — which is where disputes over 90-percent-finished framing begin.
list: Contract sum split by phase with percentages
Billing monthly or at phase completion, as stated
Lien waivers from subcontractors with each progress payment

blocks.h3: Change orders, concealed conditions and time extensions
paras: Renovation always finds something: rot behind tile, knob-and-tube wiring, a beam that is not where the drawing said. The estimate should state how concealed conditions are handled — typically a change order priced before the work proceeds, with the schedule extended accordingly.

A change order should carry the cost, the schedule impact and a signature. Contractors who proceed on a verbal "go ahead" and bill later are the ones who end up in small-claims court; the paper trail is what makes the difference, and it costs nothing to produce at the time.
list: Change order form with cost, time impact and signature
Final invoice reconciliation against the schedule of values
